items.statement:
Assume full AC. Let $F\subset S^3$ be a nonempty compact smooth embedded surface, possibly disconnected and nonorientable, every component of which has nonempty boundary. The ambient sphere has its standard orientation. The normal-transfer expression $B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)$ defines a symmetric integral bilinear pairing on the free finite-rank group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, with rational extension. It restricts on each component to its normal-transfer pairing; for cycles $a,b$ on distinct components its value is $2\operatorname{lk}(a,b)$, which need not vanish.

Suppose an embedded product cylinder $W=[-1,1]\times D^2$ meets $F$ exactly in its two end disks, on distinct components. Replace those disks by the lateral annulus and round the seams to obtain $F'$. There is an integral basis in which $B_{F'}$ has matrix $G\oplus[0]$, where $G$ is the entire matrix of $B_F$, including its cross-component entries. Thus its signature is unchanged. The boundary link and its surface collar remain fixed, so $e(F)=-\sum_i\operatorname{lk}(K_i,K_i')$, computed from boundary normal push-offs, is unchanged as well.

A finite sequence of such tubes exists making $F$ connected. All intermediate surfaces still have the original boundary link and collar, no closed components, and finite smooth disk-and-band presentations on their components. The signature and $e$ are preserved throughout.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice. Every connected compact smooth surface $F$ with nonempty boundary has a finite smooth disk-and-band presentation: it is diffeomorphic, respecting its actual boundary parametrization, to finitely many smooth disks with finitely many rectangular bands attached along pairs of disjoint boundary intervals, with compatible corner rounding. Equivalently it has a finite handle decomposition with only zero- and one-handles, all zero-handles first. The assertion allows nonorientable surfaces and twisted bands. For a smoothly embedded surface these data may be transported to the actual surface, so its disk, band and attaching charts are supplied inside that surface, rather than merely as a homotopy type.

Assume full AC. Let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth embedded surface with nonempty boundary, possibly nonorientable, with a supplied finite smooth disk-and-band presentation. The ambient three-sphere has its standard orientation. For oriented integral multicurves $a,b\subset\operatorname{int}F$, let $\tau b$ be the cycle consisting of the two small normal pushes over $b$, oriented by projection to $b$. For a one-sided circle this is one circle mapping with degree two, rather than a choice of a single normal direction. Then
$B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)$ defines a well-defined symmetric integral bilinear pairing on $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, independently of representatives and sufficiently small normal pushes. Every integral homology class has an oriented multicurve representative, permitting integer coefficients. The pairing extends to rational homology, with quadratic form $q_F(x)=B_F(x,x)$ satisfying the normal-transfer linking identity.

For an embedded compact subsurface $A\subset F$ with such a finite presentation, the pairing on $A$ is the pullback of $B_F$ under inclusion. If $F$ is oriented and its boundary is one knot, its pairing has matrix $V+V^T$ in any integral basis, where $V$ is the positive-push Seifert matrix. Orientation-preserving ambient isotopies transport the pairing.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

derivations.claim: There are finitely many components of $F$: a finite cover by connected surface charts meets them all. Apply [F1] to each, using full AC to supply countable choice. Integral cycles can be represented by oriented multicurves with integer coefficients on each component. For distinct components $A,C$, choose the normal interval neighborhood of $C$ disjoint from $A$, using compactness and [F4]. The fiber-contraction chain in [F1] then lies in the complement of every cycle $a$ on $A$ and has boundary $\tau b-2b$. Hence $\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)=2\operatorname{lk}(a,b)$ by [F2]. This is well-defined on both homology classes: a bounding chain on either component misses the other component. Its symmetry follows from [F2]. On each diagonal component summand use the pairing of [F1]. Extending these diagonal and cross terms bilinearly over $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)=\bigoplus_A H_1(A;\mathbb Z)$ proves all the pairing assertions, including equality with the total transfer expression. In particular no zero cross-term assumption has been made.

Let $A,C$ be the two distinct components at the ends of $W$, and delete the interiors of their respective end disks, giving $A_0,C_0$. Each remains connected, because paths detour around the deleted disk. Its original surface retracts onto a finite graph by collapsing the bands and disks in [F1], so its second homology is zero. Apply [F3] to the surface covered by its punctured part and a slightly enlarged removed disk. Their overlap is an annulus and its degree-zero map is injective. Exactness gives $0\to\mathbb Z\to H_1(A_0;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(A;\mathbb Z)\to0$, and the analogous sequence for $C$. The first generator is its new boundary circle. The last group is free by [F1], so both sequences split integrally, with old basis cycles chosen away from the new circles.

Cover the connected replacement of $A_0\sqcup C_0$ by that punctured pair and the lateral annulus, slightly enlarged. Their overlap is two annuli. In degree zero the two overlap generators map to $(e_A,-e_T)$ and $(e_C,-e_T)$ in $\mathbb Z\{e_A,e_C\}\oplus\mathbb Z\{e_T\}$, so this map is injective. Thus there is no additional longitudinal homology class. In degree one the overlap identifications equate the two new boundary circles, with chosen signs, to the annular core $c$. Their coefficients are units. The quotient therefore has an integral basis consisting of all old basis classes on $A,C$ together with $c$. Add the untouched components' bases. This proves $H_1(F';\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\{c\}$ with the specified old representatives. Finite smooth presentations of the replacement and untouched components exist by [F1].

The complement of $F$ is path-connected. To see this, join two complement points by a path consisting of finitely many smooth chart arcs and perturb its finitely many pieces to cross $F$ transversely in finitely many interior points, missing $\partial F$. Use finitely many chart translations with cutoff functions whose parameter derivatives span the ambient tangent space wherever the path can meet $F$. Apply [F5] simultaneously to its interior and boundary, keeping the path endpoints fixed. The boundary has codimension two, so its transverse preimage in the path is empty. Interior transversality and compact separation from the boundary give finitely many crossings. At a crossing choose an embedded arc in that surface component from the crossing to its nonempty boundary, avoiding the other finitely many crossing points. A sufficiently thin normal strip along this arc misses all other surface components. Replace the crossing path segment by a path running on one side of the strip to the boundary, round its boundary edge, and return on the other side. This detour misses $F$ and removes that crossing without creating others. The finitely many detours prove the assertion; self-intersections of this connecting path are harmless.

In the product cylinder take $c=\{0\}\times\partial D^2$ and its meridian disk $D_c=\{0\}\times D^2$. All old representatives and their sufficiently small transfers lie outside $W$; representatives avoid the end circles by step 1.2 and compactness permits those transfers. Thus $D_c$ misses their transfers, giving $B_{F'}(c,a)=0$ by [F2]. The two normal pushes of $c$ can be chosen as concentric circles of slightly smaller and larger radius in the same middle disk plane. Their linking with $c$ is zero, so $B_{F'}(c,c)=0$. All old-old entries are literally unchanged because their curves and transfers are in unchanged surface neighborhoods. This includes old classes previously on different components: their new pairing still equals their previous value $2\operatorname{lk}(a,b)$, even though they now belong to one component. Symmetry from step 1.1 proves the opposite entries zero too. The full matrix is consequently $G\oplus[0]$, with unchanged signature. The move fixes the original boundary collar, so identical normal pushes compute equal boundary self-linking numbers term by term and hence equal $e$.

If there is more than one component, choose interior points on two components, small disks there, and short normal segments from their centers to the complement. Step 2.2 joins the free ends in the complement. This can be chosen as an embedded smooth arc, fixed on the short endpoint segments: first approximate the compact complement path by a finite polygonal path in coordinate balls contained in the complement; small choices of its finitely many vertices make nonadjacent edges disjoint, since intersection of two one-dimensional segments imposes a condition of positive codimension in three-dimensional vertex space. Round its corners in disjoint smaller balls and remove any adjacent retracing. Compact separation preserves avoidance of $F$. The normal disk bundle of this interval is trivial: extend a normal frame along finitely many overlapping interval charts, rotating the frames on overlaps. Choose the end-disk parametrizations with compatible ambient orientation, so their frame discrepancy lies in the connected rotation group of an oriented plane, and correct it by a rotation along the interval. Near the endpoints first use surface-adapted coordinates $(u,v,w)$ with the surface $w=0$ and the arc its normal $w$-axis. Extend their transverse disk coordinates along the intervening compact arc by the chosen frame and [F4], joining the coordinate maps over short overlaps by cutoffs; along the axis their transverse differentials remain invertible after choosing the overlaps small. Compactness and local injectivity then give a sufficiently thin embedded product cylinder whose actual end disks lie on the two surfaces. Its interior misses $F$ by compact separation away from those endpoint charts. Its tube joins the two components, reducing their number by one and retaining all their boundary components. Repeat finitely many times. Step 3.1 preserves signature and $e$ at each stage, and [F1] supplies the finite presentations of the resulting components. This proves all conclusions.

boundaries.reason: A nonempty surface with no closed components is assumed.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 2.1 and 3.1 permit zero-rank old first homology; the new class contributes [0].
Step 3.1 computes the single new meridian class; step 4.1 includes the already connected case with no connecting moves.
Step 3.1 preserves signature even for a degenerate old pairing; no definiteness or nonsingularity is used.
Steps 3.1 and 4.1 retain the original boundary collar; tube end disks lie on distinct components.
Step 1.1 retains full AC, including countable choice for surface presentations and step 2.2 path transversality.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from normal-transfer linking and the linking-number interfaces; it supplies countable choice for the finite smooth surface presentations. Component connections and all homology calculations are finite.

risk_review.notes: Cross-component entries are 2lk, not assumed zero. MV degree-zero map is injective for distinct end components. Tubular neighborhood chosen using surface-adapted endpoint charts.

contract.proof_status_evidence: Six literal local steps, authentic complete GL1978 reading receipt, and scoped mechanical checks; independent owner review remains owed.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 The supplied presentation retracts onto a finite graph: collapse each band along its interval fibers to its core and each disk to a finite radial star joining its band intervals. These contractions agree on attaching collars and can be performed in their finite disk and rectangle charts. An integral graph cycle has a finite collection of directed edge strands, with as many incoming as outgoing strands at every vertex. Realize the strands by parallel smooth arcs in the bands, with their directions transported through any band twist, and join the ends in each vertex disk. Finite smooth arcs in a disk can be drawn with finitely many transverse crossings, by using polygonal arcs and rounding their finitely many corners. Resolve each crossing by connecting incoming to outgoing arcs in a smaller disk. This changes the cycle by a boundary in that disk and leaves a finite disjoint union of oriented embedded circles with its original homology class. A small inward displacement keeps them in the interior. This proves the representative assertion without orienting $F$. [given, construct]

1.2 The round metric gives the normal line bundle of $F$. A sufficiently short closed normal interval bundle embeds in $S^3$: the normal exponential map has invertible differential along the zero section by [F3], a finite cover gives a common positive radius, and collisions at arbitrarily small radii would converge to a single base point and contradict a local inverse there. Boundary charts are first extended slightly across the boundary, so the same argument includes their interval fibers. The inverse is smooth by induction in the derivative formula in [F3]. Denote this embedded interval bundle by $N$, and its horizontal two-sheeted boundary cover by $\pi:\widetilde F\to F$. Its total space may be connected or disconnected. Round the corners along the vertical boundary away from any chosen multicurves, producing a smooth boundary surface $\Sigma=\partial N$ that retains their horizontal lifts. Both lifts of every oriented curve are oriented by projection. No global normal direction on $F$ has been selected. [given, F3, construct]

2.1 On singular chains in $F$ define $\tau\sigma$ to be the sum of the two lifts of a simplex $\sigma$ to $\widetilde F$. A simplex is contractible by its straight-line contraction to a vertex; it is path-connected and locally path-connected. Thus [F4] gives exactly one lift for each of the two points over that vertex. Restricting lifts to any face bijects the two lift sets, again by [F4]. Consequently $\partial\tau=\tau\partial$, and $\pi_\#\tau=2\operatorname{id}$. This construction works equally for the connected and disconnected cover and uses the sum of the entire lift set. Contracting normal fibers gives, for each cycle $a$, a finite singular two-chain in $N$ with boundary $\tau a-2a$, by triangulating the finitely many simplex prisms of that homotopy. [step 1.2, F4, construct, algebra]

3.1 Define $B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)$ using the representatives in step 1.1. If $a-a'=\partial C$ on $F$, then $C$ misses $\tau b$; hence the change in linking is zero by [F1] and the symmetry in [F2]. If $b-b'=\partial D$ on $F$, step 2.1 gives $\tau b-\tau b'=\partial(\tau D)$ off $F$, so this change also has linking zero with every component of $a$. Thus the value depends only on the two homology classes. Additivity of chain transfer and of linking gives integral bilinearity. Changing to another sufficiently small positive normal radius, or to different sufficiently small transverse normal representatives, is a homotopy in the complement of $F$ through normal fibers, so [F1] proves independence of the normal push. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 To prove symmetry choose the representatives $a,b$ transverse on $F$, using finite perturbations of the disk-and-band arcs, and put $x=\tau a$, $y=\tau b\subset\Sigma$. Push a cycle on $\Sigma$ slightly outward or inward from $N$, writing superscripts $o,i$. The chain in step 2.1 misses $y^o$, since the latter is outside $N$. Therefore $2B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(x,y^o)$; here pushing $y$ outward did not meet $a$. Shifting the disjoint pair $(x,y^o)$ together inward in the boundary collar gives $(x^i,y)$, so $2B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(x^i,y)$. On the other hand $2B_F([b],[a])=\operatorname{lk}(y,x^o)=\operatorname{lk}(x^o,y)$ by [F2]. Thus their difference is $\operatorname{lk}(x^i,y)-\operatorname{lk}(x^o,y)$. Passing $x$ from the inward to the outward level crosses $y$ once for each transverse crossing of $x$ and $y$ on $\Sigma$. Its linking change is their signed surface intersection, with one fixed global sign. Indeed remove a small disk at each crossing from the traced annulus: its remaining boundary relation in the complement of $y$ expresses the change as the sum of these signed positive meridians, and [F1] evaluates each as one. Each point of $a\cap b$ has two lifts, one on each side of $F$. Their signs are opposite because the orientation of $\partial N$ induced by its outward normal reverses between the two horizontal sheets. Thus the total signed intersection of $x,y$ is zero. This proves $2B_F([a],[b])=2B_F([b],[a])$, and integral cancellation proves symmetry. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

5.1 If $F$ is oriented with one boundary knot, its transfer is the sum of positive and negative normal pushes. On a multicurve $a$, translating the disjoint pair $(a^-,a)$ together through the oriented normal collar gives $(a,a^+)$; symmetry in [F2] therefore identifies both self-linking terms. Hence $B_F([a],[a])=2\operatorname{lk}(a^+,a)$. By [F2] the right side is the quadratic form with matrix $V+V^T$. Every class has such a representative, and polarization of the symmetric bilinear forms in step 4.1 gives equality of the full pairings, not just of their diagonal values. This proves the stated matrix identification. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F2, algebra]

6.1 For a subsurface $A$, its normal line over each interior multicurve is the same as the normal line of $F$. The two transfer cycles and their linking values can therefore be chosen literally equal, proving pullback under inclusion, whether or not the inclusion on homology is injective. An orientation-preserving ambient isotopy transports the cycles and normal push homotopies and preserves their positive-meridian linking coefficients, so it transports $B_F$. Finally the finite graph in step 1.1 makes integral first homology free of finite rank; tensoring and clearing denominators extends the pairing uniquely to rational homology. Its diagonal satisfies the normal-transfer identity by step 3.1. All selections were finite within the supplied presentation, with full AC retained through the stated linking interfaces. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Proof2.1 supplies the actual fiber-contraction two-chain with boundary transfer minus twice the base cycle; Statement supplies canonical connected pairing.
